title: Japan’s birth rate rose for the first half of the year for the first time in over a decade
description: More babies follow two consecutive years of more marriages. Japan’s population has been shrinking for a long time, as fewer couples have children, and those that do have kids have fewer than generations past. But for the first time in more than a decade, there’s been an increase in the numbers of babies born in […]
content:
More babies follow two consecutive years of more marriages.

Japan’s population has been shrinking for a long time, as fewer couples have children, and those that do have kids have fewer than generations past. But for the first time in more than a decade, there’s been an increase in the numbers of babies born in Japan within the first six months of the year.

According to statistics released last week by the Japanese government’s Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare, there were 342,068 babies born between January and June of 2026, with that figure including babies born to foreign nationals in Japan. That’s 2,788 babies more than for the same period in 2025.

While that works out to a modest 0.8 percent increase, it’s still a noteworthy reversal of several consecutive years of declining birth rates. The last time Japan experienced an uptick in babies for this period compared to the previous year was all the way back in 2015. So while it’d be going to far to call 2026’s first-half increase a full-on baby boom, it’s still broken a downward trend that had been going on for 10 consecutive years, and is a pretty sizable reversal from the first half of 2025, when births were down 3.1 percent compared to the period in 2024.

▼ Births per month in 2025 (blue line) and in 2026 so far (red line)

The increase in first-half births comes on the heels of two years of increased marriages, with more couples tying the knot in both 2025 and 2024 than in the previous year. 2026 is currently tracking to make that three years in a row, with its 238,979 marriages so far 0.2 percent ahead of last year’s figure at the half-year mark. With couples choosing to have children out of wedlock still a rare occurrence in Japanese society, more couples getting married is a hopeful sign in terms of potential first-time parents contributing to the birth rate.

This doesn’t mean, though, that Japan’s population has stopped shrinking, as the 339,280 births this year is still fewer than the 778,982 deaths that have occurred. The 0.2-percent increase in births is also a small enough margin that it might not hold through the rest of the year. With any kind of birth rate increase in Japan being a rare occurrence, though, it’s still encouraging to see one finally taking place.

Source: Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare, Jiji via Yahoo! Japan News, Yomiuri Shimbun

title: Tamagotchi evolves into a ring for its 30th anniversary, preorders now open
description: This new model is the smallest one yet in the history of the egg-shaped toy that lets you raise a digital pet. Bandai’s hit digital pet device among millennial kids, the Tamagotchi, is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year. While the toy has had its ups and downs and has been reinvented many times over the […]
content:
This new model is the smallest one yet in the history of the egg-shaped toy that lets you raise a digital pet.

Bandai’s hit digital pet device among millennial kids, the Tamagotchi, is celebrating its 30th anniversary this year. While the toy has had its ups and downs and has been reinvented many times over the years, it’s currently having a clear resurgence among today’s youth, even scoring its own dedicated shop in Tokyo’s trendy Harajuku neighborhood late last year.

The newest 39th version of the main Tamagotchi series is the Tamagotchi ring. It retains the classic Tamagotchi features–egg-shaped, LCD screen, three buttons–but in its smallest form yet at only 28 millimeters (1.1 inches) long. The band, which comes with an adjustable spacer, fits Japanese ring sizes 10 through 14 comfortably.

▼ Tamagotchi Ring

For reference, the unit mounted to the Tamagotchi ring is 56 percent the size of the original Tamagotchi. Its screen is only 14.2 millimeters tall but still has all of the functions and gameplay of a regular-sized model. In addition, it’s made up of the fewest number of component parts of any full-color LCD screen-equipped Tamagotchi since the Tamagotchi + Color model was first introduced in 2008 with only 64 parts (52 electronic and 12 plastic). Even the most recently released Tamagotchi Paradise (2025) has 116 parts.

▼ (Left to right) Tamagotchi Ring (2026), Original Tamagotchi (1996), Tamagotchi + Color (2008)

While the transformation into a ring is the model’s most striking new feature, another new first in Tamagotchi history is that it comes with a dedicated charging base. Finally, in a nod to the brand’s 30th anniversary, you can grow your pet into 30 classic Tamagotchi characters from over the past three decades–including some secret ones–depending on how you raise it. Since your pet will be always be (literally) near your fingertips, that should make caring for it and unlocking all of its forms the easiest it’s ever been.

▼ (Left to right) Ball chain-style keychain (1996), wristwatch-style (2021), ring-style (2026)

The new Tamagotchi Ring comes in three colors–pink & pearl white, light blue & metallic gold, black & metallic silver–costing 7,700 yen (US$48.10) each. Preorders can now be placed on Premium Bandai’s website through October 6 at 11 p.m. JST, with orders slated to ship over two rounds in February and April 2027.

Despite our excitement at the new transformation, we still have one question regarding the naming of the new toy. Since the word “Tamagotchi” is originally a portmanteau of the words for “egg” (tamago) and “watch” (uocchi in Japanese pronunciation), “Tamagotchi ring” should logically mean something like “egg watch ring.” Wouldn’t it make more sense then just to call it the “Tamaringu” based on the Japanese pronunciation for “ring”? It’s possible that the Tamagotchi name carries too much weight at this point, but in any case, we’ll stop overthinking and get back to keeping our own digital pets alive.

title: Family Mart releases Famima convenience store products nationwide, but which ones are worth buying?
description: We review all the products to find out which ones should you try and which ones you should miss. Last month, Japanese convenience store chain Family Mart made news when it opened a new flagship in Tokyo called Famima Park Azabudai. Produced under the guidance of fashion designer and creative director Nigo, founder of streetwear […]
content:
We review all the products to find out which ones should you try and which ones you should miss.

Last month, Japanese convenience store chain Family Mart made news when it opened a new flagship in Tokyo called Famima Park Azabudai. Produced under the guidance of fashion designer and creative director Nigo, founder of streetwear brands A Bathing Ape and Human Made, the new-look store has a cool, sleek vibe to it and a slew of new products to match, also developed under Nigo’s direction.

▼ Famima Park Azabudai

While these products were only available at the flagship initially, Family Mart recently released a huge chunk of them at regular branches nationwide, so more customers can now get a taste of the “Famima” project and enjoy its original character-driven products and lifestyle items.

With well over a dozen items in the range, it’s not easy to choose between them all, and even more difficult to decide which ones are worth buying. To help you make that choice, we headed out and purchased everything in the range to give you an honest review, saving you time and reducing the overwhelm you might feel upon seeing the range in store.

▼ We’ll cover each one and rate them as BUY ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑ / TRY ⭑⭑⭑☆☆ / SKIP ⭑☆☆☆☆

▼ Let’s dip our toes into the range with the keychains, some of which are soft while others are metallic, but all of which are very tempting.

▼ 3-D Rubber Keychain F (800 yen [US$5.03])

This lightweight, rubber-type keychain features Famima’s unnamed “F” mascot character.

TRY ⭑⭑⭑☆☆

▼ The only thing holding us back from rating this a must-buy is its size, as it’s slightly bulky.

While that can be handy when you’re fishing around in your bag for your keys, when you’re out and about, and especially if you have limited room in your luggage, one of the more slimline keyrings will likely be a better fit while still being a cool convenience store souvenir.

▼ 3D Rubber Keychain – Family Mart Cafe Mini 4-Piece Set (1,400 yen)

Another lightweight design, this rubber keychain is slightly less bulky, as it has four miniature Famima-branded cups in varying sizes dangling off the main chain.

BUY ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑

This keychain gets our vote for its unique cuteness, with “Famima Cafe” written on each cup so there’s no mistaking where you got it from. Not only are they cute, they’re also very good quality, and feel great to the touch while being nice and quiet compared to metallic keychains.

▼ Metal Keychain – Family Mart Cafe Mini 4-Piece Set (1,400 yen)

A sturdy, metallic keychain that replicates Famima’s coffee cups and their corresponding sizes.

BUY ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑

This slim keychain won’t take up much room in your bag at all, and the jangly noise that the cups make as they swing against each other is delightfully pleasant.

Another surprisingly high-quality piece, this keychain also comes with the Famima logo on the reverse side of the largest cup.

▼ Metal Keychain – Famichiki (800 yen)

This sturdy keychain is designed to resemble the familiar packaging used for Family Mart’s Famichiki fried chicken.

BUY ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑

Nothing says Family Mart quite like Famichiki, arguably its most iconic signature product, making this a definite must-buy.

Made with high-quality materials, the keychain has a smooth-yet-textured surface that makes it feel nice under the fingers, and the Famima logo on the reverse side is another sweet design feature.

▼  Rubber Keychain – Famichiki (800 yen)

A lightweight rubber keychain featuring a Famichiki design.

BUY ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑

This keychain recreates the Famichiki with a plump look and feel that’s slightly more realistic compared to the metallic version.

The faithful recreation continues on the back, where you’ll find instructions on how to eat a Famichiki, just as you would on the in-store packs.

A very cool way to show your love for Famicihiki… although it might just make you crave a piece of juicy fried chicken every time you look at it.

▼ Plush Keychain – F (1,200 yen)

The “F” character appears as a plush keychain that can be hung off a bag or used as a decorative item in your room. 

SKIP ⭑☆☆☆☆

While this plush “F” is soft to touch, and fits satisfyingly in your hand, unless you’re a fan of chunky plush keychains, this is something you might want to skip. 

The “F” character is yet to become as strongly associated with Family Mart as the chain’s blue-white-and-green stripes, so although it’s cute, it doesn’t have enough of a “wow” factor yet to warrant the investment.

▼ Plush Keychain – Sun and Star (1,200 yen)

This “sun and star” keychain features what looks to be the sun, despite being a cool shade of green.

SKIP ⭑☆☆☆☆

Despite being soft and satisfying to hold, like a plush stress ball, this item just doesn’t have the right level of cuteness or recognition yet for us to wholeheartedly recommend it.

▼ Sun and Stars Tote Bag – Ivory (1,998 yen)

This bag features a versatile two-way design lets you carry it over your shoulder or by hand.

TRY ⭑⭑⭑☆☆

▼ The two-way feature makes this a handy bag to use in a variety of everyday settings.

▼ The canvas material is solid and well made, with a good quality gusset and reinforcements.

However, the sturdy construction also means it’s slightly heavy and not so easy to wash and dry, which could be an inconvenience for those travelling around Japan.

▼ Money Roll-Style Eco Bag – Light Grey (500 yen)

Generously sized, this eco bag rolls up to resemble a roll of money and is kept secure with an elastic band.

BUY ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑

The blue-white-and-green stripes are easily identifiable Family Mart markers, making this a fun convenience store souvenir that’s practical as well.

The bag, which has the Famima logo on one side, has conveniently long handles, allowing you to hold it by hand or sling it over your shoulder.

Lightweight and compact, the bag will come in handy for those times when you wind up buying more than you thought you would while out and about, saving you in a pinch.

▼ Paper shopping bag – F, Small (350 yen) and Medium (400 yen)

Stylish and simple, this paper bag has a wide base, and can be used for various occasions.

SKIP ⭑☆☆☆☆

Though it looks like a plain paper bag from a distance, when you’re up close you can make out the cute details of the “F” character.

With handles made from material, this is a good quality bag, but unless you’re in a bind and need it for gift-giving Family Mart goods, this is, in our opinion, one of the products you can skip in the collection.

▼ Ballpoint Pen – White x Green (350 yen)

This pen keeps to a simple two-tone colour scheme of white and green, with the FAMIMA logo adding a strong accent.

SKIP ⭑☆☆☆☆

While there’s certainly nothing wrong with owning a Bic Pen like this one, the other pen in the collection is more of a showstopper.

▼ Mascot Ballpoint Pen – F (880 yen)

This clip-on ballpoint pen features an eye-catching, adorable character design.

TRY ⭑⭑⭑☆☆

Made in Japan with the help of Bandai Namco, this is a quality product that’s unique as well, with nothing else quite like it on the market. Though it’s not an essential must-buy, if you are looking for a pen, this is one that’ll put a smile on your dial.

▼ Famima Cafe Tumbler (1,500 yen)

A tumbler that’s designed to hold Famima Cafe coffee cups, with both hot and cold retention properties.

SKIP ⭑☆☆☆☆

Despite being sturdy and stylish, you won’t have much need for this unless you’re a regular Family Mart coffee drinker, so this is one you could skip.

▼ Boxed Tissues – F (370 yen)

High-quality tissues, made in Japan using 100-percent pure pulp.

SKIP ⭑☆☆☆☆

This is a very good-looking box, and the tissues themselves are good quality, but it is on the large side, making it slightly impractical unless you want to add a splash of Famima flair to your home.

▼ Line Socks – Famima / White (680 yen)

Popular line socks now come in a new character color scheme, covering the following sizes: 22-25 centimetres (8.7–9.8 inches), 25-28 centimetres and children’s (13-19 centimetres, 19-22 centimetres).

BUY ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑

Family Mart socks have become an iconic way to add the chain’s brand colours to your wardrobe, and this new variety gives the striped design a unique twist, with the addition of the “F” character.

▼ The F sits on one foot only, giving the pair a fashionable, asymmetrical look.

Not only do these socks look cool, they feel fantastic too. In fact, they seem softer and more long-lasting than the chain’s regular Line Socks, making them great value for 680 yen.

▼ Imabari Towel – Sun and Star / White (800 yen)

This Imabari-made hand towel features a color scheme inspired by the sun-and-star motifs, and is highly absorbent.

TRY ⭑⭑⭑☆☆

Imabari is a highly respected Japanese towel brand, and small square towels like this are commonly used in Japan to dry your hands when using public restrooms. Against that backdrop, this little towel has a lot going for it, especially in summer when it also comes in handy for mopping sweat off your brow, so this is a little piece of Japan that you won’t regret trying.

▼ Outer T-shirt – Sun and Star / White (1,998 yen)

This limited-edition item features the Famima Sun and Star logo on an “Outer T-shirt”, an iconic item from Family Mart’s Convenience Wear line.

SKIP ⭑☆☆☆☆

This was a tough one to rate, but given its limited sizing – the shirt only comes in medium and large – and the large placement of the logo, which is yet to gain traction in the fashion community, this is a shirt you could probably skip without feeling bad about it.

It is made with a heavy cotton so there are no issues with quality, and it hangs well on the body, but if you’re going to spend close to 2,000 yen on a shirt, the plain black or white T-shirts in the Convenience Wear line will give you the same fit, but with more versatility for a wider range of occasions.

▼ Vinyl Umbrella Azabudai Map – 65 centimetres (1,480 yen)

An umbrella with a map design that shows the location of the flagship store. 

BUY ⭑⭑⭑⭑⭑

With a green handle branded with the Famima logo, this is a distinctive umbrella with a generous 65-centimetre (26-inch) diameter. 

What really makes this one special is the map design, which will take you right back to the streets of Tokyo every time you look at it.

Stylish and practical, this is a great umbrella to cheer you up on grey, rainy days, with bright Famima branding adding an accent of colour to the city streets and main location markers.

This turned out to be our favourite item in the whole collection, and we still smile every time we open it.

This truly is a massive collection for a massive name in the convenience store world, and we have a feeling that it’s just the start of even greater things for the Famima brand. Being relatively new, there’s a chance that products might be phased in and out of the collection as the brand works to carve out its niche, so if there is something that catches your eye, it’s best to grab it while you can. And you can always put together a whole look out of Convenience Wear as a side quest while you’re there!

title: Japan’s most popular curry rice restaurant chain, Coco Ichibanya, might be for sale
description: Economic and cultural factors are making it hard to make money selling one of Japan’s favorite meals. For curry rice fans, buying some Cocoichi often sounds like an appealing idea. Soon, though, someone might not only have the opportunity to purchase curry rice at Japan’s most popular curry restaurant chain, but to buy the chain […]
content:
Economic and cultural factors are making it hard to make money selling one of Japan’s favorite meals.

For curry rice fans, buying some Cocoichi often sounds like an appealing idea. Soon, though, someone might not only have the opportunity to purchase curry rice at Japan’s most popular curry restaurant chain, but to buy the chain itself.

Curry House Coco Ichibanya, to use the restaurant’s full name, was founded in Nagoya in 1978, and from the start it made use of curry roux supplied by House Foods Group. As the chain grew, House Food Group became increasingly convinced of its potential, eventually acquiring shares in Ichibanya Co., Ltd., Cocoichi’s management company. In 2015, House spent an additional 30 billion yen (US$189 million) to purchase even more Ichibanya stock, raising its share of the company from 19.5 percent to 51 percent and making it a consolidated subsidiary of House Foods Group.

Now, though, House is considering selling off its ownership stake in Ichibanya as part of a reevaluation of its business portfolio, as it attempts to refocus its resources on ventures that it feels promise higher profitable and rates of growth,

▼ How could someone be willing to say goodbye to this?

House Foods feeling like it’s tough to make money selling curry might seem strange, given that curry rice is one of the most broadly popular dishes in modern Japanese cuisine, loved by men and women both young and old. Sure enough, during its 2025 fiscal year, Ichibanya posted sales revenue of 65.5 billion yen, up 7.4 percent from the year before. At the same time, though, the company’s net income tumbled to 2.5 billion yen, a 19.2 percent drop from the year before, with increased ingredient costs cited as a major factor.

Rising materials costs put Cocoichi restaurants in a bind, because as popular as curry rice is in Japan, it’s seen as simple comfort food, not fine dining. There’s a relatively low limit to how much restaurant diners are willing to pay for it, even if the flavor is excellent. There’s also the fact that curry is a common thing for people to cook at home in Japan, and recipe sizes can be easily expanded in order to cook several days’ worth of meals at once. That creates a sort of multiplier effect where the cost savings of home-cooked curry can be enjoyed for many consecutive meals, making it even more difficult to position restaurant curry as a premium product, and in turn making it difficult for curry restaurants to offset higher ingredient costs by raising their prices.

We’ve been seeing examples of Coco Ichibanya losing customers as it raises prices since 2024, and while initially that was offset by the remaining diners spending more on a per-person basis, the math doesn’t appear to be working in the chain’s favor anymore.

The potential sale of Ichibanya is concerning for foodies in Japan, since the slipping customer numbers aren’t a result of slipping curry quality. Cocoichi’s food still tastes as good as it ever did, and similarly to when there was talk of 7-Eleven Japan being acquired by a Canadian investment group, a new owner coming in brings the possibility of tampering with the recipes that won Cocoichi its fanbase in the first place.

It should be noted, though, that House Foods Group hasn’t yet announced that Ichibanya is for sale, and in fact spokespeople for both House and Ichibanya Co., Ltd. have said that “All options are being considered, including taking Ichibanya private.” That said, if you’ve loved Cocoichi’s curry up until now, you might want to treat yourself to a plate soon, just in case some big changes are indeed on the way.

Source: Yomiuri Shimbun, Yahoo! Japan News/Kyodo

title: A real-world Pokémon Poké Ball hotel is opening in Japan at a still-secret location [Video]
description: Pokémon Sleep evolves into a whole new way to help Pokémon Trainers get some quality Zs. For travelers in Japan, when choosing a place to stay “Hotel or ryokan (traditional inn)?” is often a question that has to be answered. Now, though, there’s a new accommodation option: Poké Ball. content:
Pokémon Sleep evolves into a whole new way to help Pokémon Trainers get some quality Zs.

For travelers in Japan, when choosing a place to stay “Hotel or ryokan (traditional inn)?” is often a question that has to be answered. Now, though, there’s a new accommodation option: Poké Ball.

In a bit of a linguistic contradiction, the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel is a joint project between the Pokémon Company and hospitality design company Not a Hotel. Not a Hotel describes its philosophy as “partner[ing] with acclaimed creatives to create one-of-a-kind homes for every location,” usually resulting in luxury rental properties with avant-garde architecture and interior designs. For this latest project, though, they’re building Poké Balls big enough for humans to sleep comfortably in, a fitting endeavor for the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel’s tie-in with the Pokémon Sleep wellness app.

Of course, you wouldn’t really be able to appreciate the accurate recreation of the shape of a Poké Ball if these were just rooms inside a building, would you? So instead, guests at the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will be sleeping in detached Poké Balls in a lush natural environment, sort of a Pokémon glamping experience.

As for exactly where Poké-travelers will be staying, that’s still being kept a secret. All that’s been revealed so far is that the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will be “somewhere in Hokkaido,” Japan’s northernmost prefecture. With Hokkaido boasting some of Japan’s lushest forests, the prefecture has no shortage of locations that could evoke the feeling of being on an adventurous journey to become a Pokémon Master, so its hard to speculate on any more specific location at the moment.

We probably won’t have to wait too long, though, since reservations are scheduled to open on September 15, at which time assumedly the exact location of the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will be revealed. Speaking of its name, the use of the term “Poké Ball,” instead of “Monster Ball” as the items are called in Japanese-language Pokémon media, implies that the hotel will be welcoming of international travelers, and with Hokkaido getting enough snow in midwinter to make semi-outdoor accommodations an unappealing prospect, odds are the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will be looking to welcome its first guests very soon.

title: Finally! Japan’s big three convenience store chains announce rice ball price reductions
description: After years of going up, onigiri prices are starting to come down. Onigiri (rice balls) used to be a Japanese convenience store item with no real downside. Tasty, filling, and healthier than just about any other snack on the shelves, they were also very reasonably priced, with most varieties costing about 120-140 yen (roughly US$0.75 […]
content:
After years of going up, onigiri prices are starting to come down.

Onigiri (rice balls) used to be a Japanese convenience store item with no real downside. Tasty, filling, and healthier than just about any other snack on the shelves, they were also very reasonably priced, with most varieties costing about 120-140 yen (roughly US$0.75 to US$0.90), so really the only reason not to buy one was if you were already completely full.

This paradise, though, was not to last. As rice prices started rising, convenience stores continually increased the price of their onigiri, and they now often cost roughly double compared to what they did just a few years ago.

But now, finally, onigiri prices are starting to come down, as Japan’s three largest convenience store chains, 7-Eleven, Family Mart, and Lawson, have all recently announced rice ball price reductions. There aren’t limited-time sales, either, but revisions to the onigiri’s base prices to make them more affordable.

From September 29, Lawson will be knocking 10 yen off the after-tax price of all of its Temaki Onigiri. That means the Sea Chicken Mayonnaise goes from 181 yen back down to 171, the ume (plum), kombu, and okaka (bonito flake) onigiri each from 194 to 184, the grilled salmon onigiri from 221 to 211, and the mentaiko (spicy cod roe) from 235 to 225. Special region-specific Temaki Onigiri will also become 10 yen cheaper, with the reduced prices applying to a total of 20 different rice ball varieties.

7-Eleven Japan’s onigiri repricing isn’t as extensive, but it will be lowering the prices of its salmon and mentaiko onigiri, which currently have after-tax prices of 214 yen, by 19 yen. Family Mart, meanwhile, has already lowered the price of its Kombu and Tuna Mayonnaise Big Musubi rice ball from 320 yen to 298, as of August 24.

The price of rice itself finally coming down is no doubt a big factor in the lowered onigiri prices. According to a study by the Japanese government’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, the average price for a five-kilogram (11-pound) bag of rice actually sold at supermarkets dropped 27.7 percent between the start of this year and mid-August. Obviously 7-Eleven, Lawson, and Family Mart are getting the rice for their onigiri from wholesalers, not their local grocery store, but the ministry’s statistics still point to rice prices in general having come down significantly over the past few months.

It would probably be giving convenience stores too much credit to say that they’ve lowered their onigiri prices out of the goodness of their hearts, as they are, after-all, profit-motivated business entities. With many shoppers balking at the severely increased prices for what was once an impulse-buy with no thought or guilt required, lowering onigiri prices has the potential to actually increase the stores’ revenue if it helps entice people into buying them once again, even if there’s still a long way to go before rice balls are close to what their pre-kooky prices were.

One thing to keep in mind regarding Lawson’s sweeping price reduction is that it only applies to their Temaki Onigiri series of rice balls in which the rice ball doesn’t come with its seaweed covering directly wrapped around the rice, which can make the packaging a little tricky to open for those not used to it, but we can help you get up to speed.

Source: Asahi Shimbun via Golden Times, Jiji, Gourmet Watch via Yahoo! Japan News

title: Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon Ice Cream makes us rethink everything we thought we knew about sweets
description: This noodle dessert makes our brains malfunction. When it comes to Kagawa, udon is king. Not only is the climate ideal for growing wheat – udon is a wheat noodle – but locals in Kagawa eat more udon per person than anywhere else in Japan, leading it to be dubbed Japan’s “Udon Prefecture”, a moniker […]
content:
This noodle dessert makes our brains malfunction.

When it comes to Kagawa, udon is king. Not only is the climate ideal for growing wheat – udon is a wheat noodle – but locals in Kagawa eat more udon per person than anywhere else in Japan, leading it to be dubbed Japan’s “Udon Prefecture”, a moniker that Kagawa proudly stands by.

We were reminded of just how strong the links are between noodles and the prefecture when, on a recent trip to the area, we spotted a sign outside a beautiful old shop along the approach to Kompirasan, one of the region’s most famous shrines.

▼ The sign, posted at the Konpira Udon Sando Store, read: “Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon-style Soft Serve”.


Having travelled to different parts of Japan, we knew that turning local specialties into ice cream has become something of a thing in recent years, but we were surprised to see udon being used this way. Making it even more unusual was the fact that the ice cream was based on onsen egg bukkake udon, one of our favourite noodle dishes. As fans of the dish, we were curious to find out how well the ice cream could replicate its look and flavour, so we decided to step into the shop and order a real onsen egg bukkake udon and the soft serve to see how they would compare.

▼ Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon at 730 yen (US$4.90) on the left, Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon-style Soft Serve (580 yen) on the right.

It only took about five minutes for both dishes to arrive, and when they did, we were charmed by how the shape and size of the bowls were almost identical.

▼ What wasn’t identical, though, was what was inside them.

There, on the right, was a bowl of white goodness that had a noodly look to it, and on top, a slice of lemon and the onsen egg, two ingredients you would usually find in a bowl of Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon.

▼ Look closely and you’ll see a splash (“bukkake” means “splash”) of sauce resembling soy sauce-based dashi within the “noodles”.

The presentation was so convincing in person that we momentarily forgot this was ice cream until we saw the dessert spoon there in place of chopsticks. Resisting the urge to gobble it down right away, we stopped to try the actual noodles on the left hand side of the tray.

▼ Absolutely delicious.

Kagawa udon truly is something else – the noodles had a wonderfully firm and slippery texture, and the balance of the dashi was perfect. After gently breaking the onsen egg apart and mixing it through the noodles, the flavour became smoother and richer, with the oil from the tempura crumbs and aroma of green onions adding just the right amount of texture and freshness to the dish.

▼ Time to try the Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon-style Soft Serve.

Releasing the yolk on this dish felt entirely wrong because, well…when would you normally break an egg over ice cream? Still, this is exactly how the dish is meant to be eaten, so we watched as the orange yolk slowly flowed over the white cream, creating an unorthodox, and sinful-looking, dessert.

▼ Gently mixing some of the yolk into the ice cream, we lifted a spoonful up for a taste, and…

▼ …what the heck is this?

The richness and saltiness of the yolk subdued the sweetness of the cream, shifting the flavour from something that felt like a dessert towards something more like a meal. We never imagined that egg yolk and ice cream would work so well together, but when we stopped to think about it, we realised that both custard and ice cream contain egg yolk, so perhaps the pairing makes perfect sense. Still, there was something entirely different about eating ice cream with a runny onsen egg oozing over it, and though it was odd, it wasn’t bad at all.

Curious to find out how lemon would affect the flavours, we first squirted some on the real noodle dish to get a sense of the taste.

▼ Yep, a classic combination that’s totally delicious.

We then  squeezed the lemon over our onsen egg ice cream, and…

▼… this worked surprisingly well too!

As soon as the acidity came into play, the finish became much lighter, lifting the sweet and salty richness of the dessert with a delicious freshness. It was genuinely a new and interesting kind of dessert, and so good that we could see ourselves becoming seriously addicted to it.

The flavour was so captivating that we interspersed the experience with mouthfuls of udon, which really broke our brain.

▼ Udon!

▼ Soft serve!


▼ Udon!!

▼ Soft serve!!!

Eventually, our taste buds started to become very confused, and at that point our brain malfunctioned and we wound up doing the unthinkable: we mixed the udon and ice cream together. This turned out be another surprise, as the two dishes worked together far better than expected, and we easily polished off the whole thing.

By the end of our very unorthodox meal, we realised two things. First, the Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon-style Soft Serve is an udon-inspired dessert that does a very good job of looking like a noodle dish. Secondly, we’ve rarely ever eaten a dessert with this level of attention to detail before.

From making it look like udon, which is no easy feat when you’re working with a soft ingredient, right through to the bowl and presentation, and the idea to include the onsen egg and lemon, which transforms the flavour while you eat, every element has clearly been carefully designed for the diner’s enjoyment.

Even when eaten alongside our beloved onsen egg bukkake udon, the soft serve held its own as a dessert, and we highly recommend trying it if you can. It’ll become a dessert to remember, and a nice way to reward yourself after climbing the shrine’s 785 stairs.

title: Japan Railways announces unlimited-ride train pass for fall travel
description: A great way to explores off-the-beaten-path Japan this autumn. You can make a strong argument that fall is the best time of year to travel in Japan. In summer you’ve got heat, humidity, rainstorms, and large crowds of both domestic and international tourists to contend with. In spring, you might also run into crowds and […]
content:
A great way to explores off-the-beaten-path Japan this autumn.

You can make a strong argument that fall is the best time of year to travel in Japan. In summer you’ve got heat, humidity, rainstorms, and large crowds of both domestic and international tourists to contend with. In spring, you might also run into crowds and inflated hotel prices because of the cherry blossoms, and, while winter tends to be the least crowded season, that’s largely because many parts of Japan aren’t much fun to be in when it’s cold and snowy.

Autumn, though, comes with hardly any of those downsides, and now it’s looking like an even better season in which to explore the country thanks to the announcement by JR/Japan Railways Group of its new Unlimited Autumn Ride rail pass.

Called the Aki no Norihodai Pass in Japanese, this deal gives you three full days of unlimited rides on JR regular and rapid (kaisoku) trains. There aren’t any regional restrictions, either – the pass lets you ride regular and kaisoku trains on any JR line in Japan.

There is a catch, in that the pass doesn’t get you onto express and special express trains, so it can’t be used on the Shinkansen. With many of Japan’s standard-itinerary sightseeing attractions along the major bullet train routes dealing with overtourism these days, however, there’s a lot of value in taking the time to explore off-the-beaten-path parts of country via its more local lines, and the Unlimited Autumn Ride pass also gives you unlimited rides on JR-managed BRT highway buses.

The pass is priced at 7,850 yen (US$49) for adults and 3,920 yen for children, so it shouldn’t be hard to get your money’s worth out of it on an extended-weekend trip. For travelers headed up to Japan’s northernmost prefecture, Hokkaido, there’s also a Hokkaido Shinkansen Option ticket (4,650 yen for adults, 2,320 yen for kids) that can be used in tandem with the pass and allows for a one-time ride between Shin Aomori and Kikonai Stations on the Hokkaido Shinkansen line and one ride on the non-JR Donan Isaribi Tetsudo Line from Kikonai to Goryokaku Station, from which JR lines can be accessed.

The passes will be on sale from September 18 to October 16 at major JR stations, JR travel centers, and third-party travel agencies and can be used for a period of three consecutive days between October 3 and 18.

title: Lawson convenience store opens its first mobile, trailer-style location in Japan
description: The new mobile model is also being considered for use in disaster-stricken areas. The future of Japanese convenience stores may be on wheels. Located at the south side of the gymnasium at Ebina Sports Park in Kanagawa Prefecture, a new type of trailer-style Lawson convenience store opened for business on August 27. It’s slated to […]
content:
The new mobile model is also being considered for use in disaster-stricken areas.

The future of Japanese convenience stores may be on wheels.

Located at the south side of the gymnasium at Ebina Sports Park in Kanagawa Prefecture, a new type of trailer-style Lawson convenience store opened for business on August 27. It’s slated to be in operation through March 31 as the chain tests its viability to make an impact on the market. Not having a fixed physical building lowers the cost and allows the chain to make inroads in places that were previously inaccessible and lacking konbini, as Japanese convenience stores are fondly nicknamed. Plus, as it’s portable and relatively easy to set up, officials are taking into account its serious potential to be at the forefront of relief efforts for when disasters such as earthquakes strike across the country.

▼ The new trailer-style Lawson konbini

The interior is about one-fifth the size of an ordinary Lawson store with a total length of 12.2 meters (40 feet).  It carries around 500 items for sale including prepared foods such as bento, onigiri, fried foods, and desserts, as well as drinks and other daily necessities. A 6.1-meter (20-foot) long kitchen/office space is also attached where the foods are prepared. However, some things have to go given the limited space, so this branch is missing the usual ATM, copy machine, and Loppi ticket kiosk found at regular Lawson store locations.

▼ The total area of the store space is a snug 33.60 square meters (361.7 square feet).

Time will tell if this new type of Lawson proves viable in the long run among the already oversaturated konbini market with new contenders popping up every so often. However, given the weight of Lawson’s name as one of the “Big 3” konbini and the uniquely positioned ability of this mobile model to be accessible in times of need, we’ll tentatively say that it looks like the future’s on wheels.

title: The mystery of Port Store, the Japanese convenience store that looks like a Lawson rip-off
description: What looks like an anime convenience store is actually a heartwarming way to serve the local community. All the big-name convenience stores in Japan have instantly recognisable features that can easily be identified from a distance, and for Lawson, that means blue, white and pink stripes, and a distinctive milk can logo. Well, we thought […]
content:
What looks like an anime convenience store is actually a heartwarming way to serve the local community.


All the big-name convenience stores in Japan have instantly recognisable features that can easily be identified from a distance, and for Lawson, that means blue, white and pink stripes, and a distinctive milk can logo.

Well, we thought that was the case until our reporter Mr Sato stumbled upon this store in Aomi, just a stone’s throw from Tokyo’s famous Odaiba district.

▼ From a distance, this looks like a regular Lawson.

▼ But as you get closer…

▼ … you realise it’s something different.

The store looks identical to a Lawson – so much so that if you’re not paying attention you might even walk through its doors thinking as such, but look closely and you’ll see the words “Port Store” on the sign instead of Lawson.

▼ Even the milk can logo has “Port Store” branding.

A sight like this is enough to make you think you’ve stepped out of reality and into a parallel universe, because convenience stores are notoriously protective of their trademarks, and would never let a store like this rip off their branding in the real world.

▼ Yet here it is, existing like something out of an anime or video game, with everything telling you it’s a Lawson, except for the name.

Sensing he may have found a glitch in the system, Mr Sato walked towards the Port Store and stepped through its automatic doors.

Looking around, his brain short-circuited again, as he saw that the selections on offer were more or less the same as what you’d find at a regular Lawson. However, there were some products that appeared to be unique to this location, including work gloves, socks and towels, and work shoes and helmets.

Stopping for a moment, Mr Sato whipped out his phone and ran a search online to find out exactly what he had walked into, and that’s when he learned that the store is operated by the Tokyo Port Welfare Association in partnership with Lawson. The association is a non-profit that runs shops and other services for people working in Tokyo’s port areas, and by partnering with convenience stores like Lawson and Family Mart it was able to expand, providing port workers with easier access to essential work gear and leading to the “Port Store” branded convenience stores seen in some port areas today.

Being able to buy items normally sold at workwear stores is convenient for people who work in these areas, especially when these stores are open 24 hours. For Mr Sato, though, the store had three things that lured him into opening his wallet – a waffle cone milk ice cream, cheap cheese crackers, and a Toraichi towel.

Toraichi is a Japanese workwear brand, particularly well known among manual labourers, and something you normally wouldn’t find at a convenience store.

▼ Mr Sato, looking and feeling cool with his ice cream and Toraichi towel.

While the store caters to port workers, you don’t have to be a port worker to make a purchase, so Mr Sato highly recommends stopping by if you ever see one during your travels. It’s a unique take on the Japanese convenience store and a nice reminder of how big-name chains can adapt their brand to serve the needs of the local community.

title: Japan’s revolving sushi restaurant king Sushiro coming to U.S. this fall with high prices, no tipping
description: Sushiro, budget-friendly in Japan, is adding private rooms and full-course meals as it arrives in America for the first time. Among Japan’s major kaiten/revolving sushi restaurant chains, Sushiro has the most passionate fans. Pretty much wherever a new Sushiro branch opens, you can expect crowds of sushi lovers looking to grab a seat at peak […]
content:
Sushiro, budget-friendly in Japan, is adding private rooms and full-course meals as it arrives in America for the first time.

Among Japan’s major kaiten/revolving sushi restaurant chains, Sushiro has the most passionate fans. Pretty much wherever a new Sushiro branch opens, you can expect crowds of sushi lovers looking to grab a seat at peak dining times, and this fall, for the first time, that’s probably going to be happening in America too.

Sushiro is just a few weeks away from opening its first-ever U.S. branch, and it’s not timidly testing the waters with a low-key launch in a low-competition market. Instead, it’s starting its American endeavor in New York’s Times Square.

▼ Though it was probably based more on real estate availability than issuing a direct challenge, America’s first Sushiro is located right next door to a McDonald’s.

Sushiro is leaning into its legacy of success in promoting the new restaurant, billing itself in English as the “world’s #1 sushi brand.” And yes, in some ways the preview images look similar to Sushiro branches in Japan, with large monitors near the entrance displaying the call numbers of parties whose tables are ready, and horizontally oriented touch panels with images of sushi digitally flowing by which can be tapped on to place orders.

However, there are a number of ways in which dining at Sushiro in the U.S. is going to be very different from eating at the chain’s restaurants in Japan. For one thing, Sushiro America appears to be trying to position itself as a much more premium dining destination. A two-piece plate of maguro (tuna) sushi, for example, will cost you 180 yen at Sushiro in Tokyo. In New York, though, a plate of maguro will cost US$5, equivalent to roughly 800 yen.

Granted, restaurant prices are higher in general in America than they are in Japan, and the current exchange rate makes the gap feel even bigger. That said, assuming a person were to eat five plates of maguro, that 900 yen would still be considered a rather modestly priced restaurant meal in Japan, whereas a $25 meal in the U.S., while not a major luxury in today’s economy, isn’t a particularly thrifty meal either. There’s also the fact that the New York Sushiro’s maguro will actually be cheaper than its other types of sushi, which will be priced at 6, 8, or 10 dollars a plate.

Further signs of Sushiro’s upscale American dream can be found in the New York branch’s private rooms, something not seen in chain revolving sushi restaurants in Japan. Located on a separate level of the restaurant from the other diners, each room has swanky minimalist décor and its own refined name, such as “Sho Chiku Bai,” “Wabi Sabi,” or “Yama Kawa Umi.”

If you’re wondering where the lanes that whisk your food to you are hidden in these private rooms, there aren’t any. Sushro says that these rooms provide patrons with “a Japanese private dining experience featuring a curated prix fixe course menu.”

That doesn’t mean no care will be given to the main dining area’s automatically delivered dishes, though, and Sushiro boasts that customers will be able to choose from some 200 menu items. Some of these will be original creations crafted specifically to cater to American tastes, such as a double-cheeese shrimp roll and marinated salmon with cream cheese.

▼ It’s also kind of unusual that Sushiro America is trying to make “Eat ‘til you drop” its catchphrase. Not only is the chain not known for large portions, the Japanese phrase kuidaore, which literally means “eat until you drop,” is already associated with the city of Osaka and its food culture as a whole, not just Sushiro’s Osaka-based parent company.

But while the Sushiro experience in America is going to have some differences from the one in the chain’s home country, there is one surprising way it’s going to be just like in Japan. The management has put the word out that the New York Sushiro will have a no-tipping policy, with the announcement being greeted with a round of applause by attendees at a preview event, reflecting a growing sense of fatigue among American consumers towards gratuities.

Sushiro’s New York branch is slated to open sometime this coming October.

title: Elderly couple donates 400 million yen to erect Myaku-Myaku statue in Osaka
description: Multi-million-dollar Myaku-Myaku donation. It’s been nearly a year since the closing of the 2025 World Expo in Osaka, but its official mascot, the gooey humanoid Myaku-Myaku has managed to secure a popularity that has transcended the event it was created to represent. Myaku-Myaku goods are still widely sold, and game centers are still well stocked […]
content:
Multi-million-dollar Myaku-Myaku donation.

It’s been nearly a year since the closing of the 2025 World Expo in Osaka, but its official mascot, the gooey humanoid Myaku-Myaku has managed to secure a popularity that has transcended the event it was created to represent. Myaku-Myaku goods are still widely sold, and game centers are still well stocked with crane games offering chances at plush toys and other goods bearing its moist likeness.

It’s a rather surprising turn of events for the mascot after its debut in 2022, which left people unsure of how to feel about its characteristics, both cute, such as its big smile and stubby little legs, and grotesque, such as its head looking like bloody entrails.

▼ Early Myaku-Myaku fan art.

シニゲーくん pic.twitter.com/kiBndmNDva

— 色紙の妖精しきっしー (@SIKISSYfacerock) April 26, 2022

But over the years, people by and large seemed to really warm up to Myaku-Myaku. Its post-Expo activities have only continued to grow into projects such as a tastefully erotic photo book.

And now, a surprise donation to the City of Osaka may very well cement the mascot’s legacy for generations to come. Reports have recently come in that business owner Keihachi Fukunishi and his wife Akiyo Fukunishi, both 85, have given 200 million yen each, for a total of 400 million (US$2.5 million) yen to the city.

▼ There were already several statues at the venue, but the materials weren’t intended for permanent use.

The couple’s donation came with a request that a statue of Myaku-Myaku be erected on the site where the Expo was held. At a press event where Keihachi and Akiyo received letters of appreciation, the husband told reporters the Myaku-Myaku “is a symbol. Just as the Tower of the Sun defined the Senri Expo Park, Myaku-Myaku defines the Osaka-Kansai Expo.”

He makes an interesting comparison too. The Tower of the Sun was the centerpiece of the 1970 Expo, which was also held in Osaka and also wasn’t without controversy when first unveiled. Its creator, Taro Okamoto, created it in almost direct opposition to the post-moon-landing Expo’s overarching theme of technological progress by filling his statue with organic and tribalistic imagery.

▼ The Tower of the Sun

However, by the end of that Expo, it was widely lauded as a masterpiece and still stands today, designated as a national tangible cultural property. Perhaps Myaku-Myaku’s own shockingly organic appearance and subsequent rise to prominence reminded the Fukunishis of the Tower of the Sun, and they wanted to entrench the mascot’s legacy in the same way.

In response, Osaka mayor Hideyuki Yokoyama said, “I would like to accelerate deliberation so that Myaku-Myaku can take its place alongside the Grand Ring as a new symbol of this site.”

Another of the Expo’s highlights was the massive wooden Grand Ring that encompassed much of the venue and measured about two kilometers (1.2 miles) in circumference. All but a 200-meter stretch of it has been slated for demolition to make room for Japan’s first integrated resort and casino, which will be built next to a commemorative park that honors the Expo.

However, many readers of the news online were irked by Yokoyama’s promise to “accelerate deliberation” (kento wo kasoku), a typical non-committal phrase used by politicians to essentially say, “We’ll think about whether we want to do this or not as soon as we can.” On the other hand, some wonder if building a giant Myaku-Myaku statue might end up costing the people of Osaka in the long run.

“So, will they give the money back if they decide not to do it after their accelerated deliberations?”
“What is this accelerated deliberation nonsense? Just get it going so it’s built in time for that elderly couple to see it!”
“I hate hearing ‘accelerate deliberation,’ because it means it’ll probably never happen.”
“They’d do a lot more good by donating that money to fix the many deteriorating drainage pumps in the southern part of the city.”
“I wonder if the donors thought about maintenance costs. Seems a bit arrogant to me.”
“If they love Myaku-Myaku so much, why not build the statue in their own home?”
“Asking for a Myaku-Myaku statue just because you donate money gives me the same unsettling vibes as a corporation donating money for certain favors.”
“That’s a wonderful idea. They probably decided to donate the money while they’re still alive rather than just have it taken in inheritance taxes.”

The theory in that last comment seems very plausible. Given the age of the donors, it is entirely possible that they have no one who they need to leave the money to. Even if they do have heirs, a large chunk gets taken out in taxes, so why not pre-empt that along with a request as to how they’d like to see it spent?

They didn’t even say all the money needed to go into the statue, just that they’d like that to be done as a part of the donation. That being said, the idea of a giant Statue-of-Liberty-style Myaku-Myaku in the harbor of Osaka, defining the city’s skyline and welcoming everyone arriving by air and sea, is very appealing to me, and I’m not even that big a fan of the character.

title: Starbucks Japan reveals new Tsukimi Moon-Viewing drinkware and gifts for autumn 2026
description: New “Bunny Autumn Festival” collection celebrates the rabbit in the moon with sweet design details.  As we enter September, people across the nation are beginning to take notice of the encroaching night sky and the beauty of the moon, which appears particularly bright at this time of year. The moon-gazing culminates in Tsukimi (literally “moon-viewing“), […]
content:
New “Bunny Autumn Festival” collection celebrates the rabbit in the moon with sweet design details. 

As we enter September, people across the nation are beginning to take notice of the encroaching night sky and the beauty of the moon, which appears particularly bright at this time of year. The moon-gazing culminates in Tsukimi (literally “moon-viewing“), a cultural event that occurs around the time of the autumn full moon – this year the date is 25 September – and over at Starbucks, the celebrations have begun with a brand new Tsukimi collection.

Called “Bunny Autumn Festival“, the range taps into another celestial-related belief – that the markings on the moon look like a rabbit pounding rice. If you’ve ever held that image in your mind while gazing at the moon in Japan, you’ll see how the markings really do look more like a rabbit as opposed to a “man on the moon”, and it’s a beautiful way for companies like Starbucks to give moon-viewing goods an extra dash of cuteness.

The new range centres around the idea of a family of rabbits joyously celebrating the harvest festival, playing with mooncakes on a moonlit night. Though mooncakes aren’t commonly eaten here as they are in other parts of Asia, they add colour and cuteness to the collection while celebrating the moon that shines down on us all.

▼ The collection begins with the Stainless Steel To-Go Bottle, Rabbit Ivory – 473 millilitres (16 ounces) – 5,350 yen (US$33.42)

Shaped like a giant Starbucks cup, this stainless steel bottle features a locking lid for leak-proof peace-of-mind. The lid opens easily by pressing the button down and sliding it to the right.

The double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless steel construction provides excellent heat and cold retention, while the bunnies on the front provide excellent cuteness.

▼ Stainless Steel Tumbler with Replacement Lid, MiiR Rabbit Navy, 473 millilitres – 5,900 yen

The deep navy colour, reminiscent of the night sky, serves to highlight the rabbits, which can be seen leaping playfully across the bottom of the tumbler.

This item also boasts double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless steel construction, and is produced in collaboration with MiiR, a premium Seattle-based drinkware brand.

▼ Cold Cup Tumbler – 710 millilitres 3,050 yen

This product brings an air of sophistication to the range, with a starry, textured surface that catches the light, creating a beautiful, sparkly shine.

▼ The large 710-millilitre size allows you to enjoy more of your favourite beverage for longer.

▼ Cold Cup Tumbler, Rabbit Navy – 710 millilitres 2,700 yen

▼ This beautiful design features a full moon, with rabbits racing around it, against a dark night sky.

The removable lid makes this one particularly easy to clean, and like the three other items above, it comes with a free drink ticket.

▼ Stainless Steel Mug, Rabbit Coral Pink – 473 millilitres 4,200 yen

Those who prefer to drink Starbucks from a mug will be able to opt for this stylish stainless steel design, which features a wonderfully serene moment, with three bunnies gathered together under a golden moon.

▼ Double-walled vacuum insulation, and a removable lid to keep your drink hot, or cold, for longer.

Rounding out the collection are a couple of bear-y cute gifts, featuring the chain’s Bearista character.

▼ Bearista Message Gift (with drink ticket) 1,650 yen

▼ For this outing, the Bearista is dressed up in an adorable bunny costume.

The Bearista has magnets concealed in both hands, which allows it to hold the message card drink ticket firmly in place for premium presentation.

▼ It also has a loop between its ears so you can attach a keychain and use it as a charm.

The drink ticket itself is also beautifully designed, with golden embossed print and three cute rabbits under the green mermaid, surrounded by stars like a Starbucks moon.

▼ Completing the set is a gift bag so cute you’ll want to gift it to yourself.

▼ Beverage Card (with drink ticket) 750 yen

Shout someone a drink with the assistance of the sweet rabbit family, appearing on a coral-pink card that captures the fun and cosiness of moon-viewing season.

With so many different products at different price points, you don’t have to spend a lot to join the fun of moon-viewing at Starbucks this year. You’ll have to act like a bunny and jump quick, though, as the range became available online on 1 September, and at Starbucks stores on 2 September, and is only available in limited numbers while stocks last.

description: Maps and predicated peak color dates to help you plan your autumn journey to see Japan’s natural beauty. content:
Maps and predicated peak color dates to help you plan your autumn journey to see Japan’s natural beauty.

There are a lot of reasons why fall is a great time of year to travel in Japan, such as sunny weather, not-too-hot, not-too-cold temperatures, and smaller crowds. The absolute best reason for an autumn trip, though, is to see the beautiful fall colors.

In particular, Japan’s maple and ginkgo trees, or kaede and icho if you’re using their Japanese names, are what turn many of the country’s forests, gardens, and temples into a patchwork of vivid reds and yellows every autumn. Of course, there’s a timing element involved in seeing fall foliage. Head out to see it too early, and the leaves will still be in their summer-green state, but go too late, and you run the risk of the leaves being brown and withered, or maybe even having fallen off, leaving you looking at bunches of barren branches.

So to help travelers coordinate their travel plans with Mother Nature’s, Japan Meteorological Corporation has prepared a fall foliage forecast. Generally speaking, the fall colors sweep across Japan in the opposite direction that the cherry blossoms do, starting in the north, where cooler weather sets in earlier, and then moving down to east Japan, followed by the western part of the country. There’s an additional wrinkle, though, in that high-altitude areas, typically further inland from the coastline, also tend to see their leaves change color earlier than lower-lying areas.

First, let’s take a look at the forecast maps showing when the leaves are predicted to be at their most breathtakingly bright shades of red and yellow.

▼ Peak maple color forecast map showing Sapporo (札幌), Sendai (仙台), Tokyo (東京), Nagoya (名古屋), Osaka (大阪), and Fukuoka (福岡)

▼ Peak ginkgo color forecast, also with Sapporo (札幌), Sendai (仙台), Tokyo (東京), Nagoya (名古屋), Osaka (大阪), and Fukuoka (福岡)

Compared to an average year, JMC is predicting that east Japan will turn crimson later than usual, and northern Japan’s yellow leaves will be arriving later as well. In addition to the above maps, they’ve also put together a list of the peak color dates by city.

● Predicted peak color for maple/ginkgo trees
Sapporo: November 7/November 6
Aomori: November 13/November 6
Sendai: November 25/November 29
Tokyo: November 29//November 26
Kanazawa: November 30/November 10
Nagano: November 20//November 14
Nagoya: December 2//November 17
Kyoto: December 11/November 27
Osaka: December 4/November 24
Wakayama: December 11/November 26
Hiroshima: November 28//November 20
Kochi: December 9/November 16
Fukuoka: December 7/November 27
Kagoshima: December 10/November 27

As we can see from the predicted dates, gingko trees usually reach their peak color before maples, so does this mean you’ll have to pick between seeing one or the other? Not necessarily. Unlike the cherry blossoms, which appear for only a bittersweetly short time, the fall colors can be enjoyed for a longer period. Sure, it can be tricky to time a trip to see both the maples and gingko at their absolute prettiest condition at the same place at the same time, but there’s enough overlap so that if one of the leaf types is looking its best, the other is probably very photogenic too. JMC is predicting this year’s overall fall color season to be:

● North Japan
Maple: Early October to mid-November in mountains, mid-October to late November in flatlands
Ginkgo: Early November to late November in flatlands
● East Japan
Maple: Late October to early December in mountains, late November to mid-December in flatlands
Ginkgo: Early November to early December in flatlands
● West Japan
Maple: Late October to early December in mountains, late November to mid-December in flatlands
Ginkgo: Mid-November to early December in flatlands

As we’re still at least a month away from the first signs of fall color, JMC will be updating its predictions as we get deeper into fall, but for now the forecast is enough to start forming plans from. And if you just can’t wait that long for your fall trip, Japan Railways has a new unlimited-ride train pass that can be activated from early October.

Source: Japan Meteorological Corporation, PR Times

title: Mini CRT-lookalike Final Fantasy figurines are awesome pixel art music boxes [Video]
description: Square Enix’s Mini Melody TVs tap into the nostalgia for retro games and old-school electronics. With retro games, there’s often a fine yet indistinct line between games’ whose aesthetics have been canonized as timelessly charming and cultural milestones of digital artistry, and those whose graphics and sounds now merely feel antiquated, making them past their […]
content:
Square Enix’s Mini Melody TVs tap into the nostalgia for retro games and old-school electronics.

With retro games, there’s often a fine yet indistinct line between games’ whose aesthetics have been canonized as timelessly charming and cultural milestones of digital artistry, and those whose graphics and sounds now merely feel antiquated, making them past their expiration date in terms of triggering a warm, fuzzy emotional response. Tapping into gaming nostalgia gets trickier still when you take into account that many fans’ memories aren’t tied only to the games themselves, but to the equipment they were played with, much of which has also now been replaced by newer tech.

So it’s nice to see Square Enix going the extra mile in presenting the Final Fantasy series’ early sights and sounds with these cool, clever figurines that look like CRT television sets.

The Final Fantasy Series–Mini Melody TV collection takes us back to Final Fantasy’s initial pixel art era, consisting of the first six games in the series, which were released for the NES/Famicom and Super NES/Super Famicom. Each figurine’s screen shows a scene from one of the games and also plays an iconic piece of background music from its soundtrack.

For the original Final Fantasy, you’ll see the title screen (which, famously, doesn’t come until after you complete the first objective of our quest) and its rousing musical accompaniment that would go on to become the main theme of Final Fantasy.

Final Fantasy II’s figurine plays “The Rebel Army,” and Final Fantasy III’s “Eternaal Wind.”

The Final Fantasy IV Mini Melody TV shows us Cecil, still in dark knight mode, sailing through the skies to “The Red Wings,” while Final Fantasy V’s recaptures Bartz party’s battle with Gilgamesh, backed by “Battle at the Big Bridge,” a frantic fight theme that’s possibly the most widely remembered thing about the entire game.

And finally, the Final Fantasy VI figurine has us checking in on Setzer, Celes, Edgar, and Sabin aboard the airship Falcon, searching for their lost friends as, fittingly, “Searching for Friends” plays.

Each of the figurines draws power from a AAA battery to light up its screen, which is actually an LCD display, despite the CRT-style casing. With dimensions of 6.2 x 4.45 x 5.3 centimeters (2.4 x 1.3 x 2.1 inches), they’re compact enough to fit more than one on your desk, and you may want to pick up more than one, since they’re being offered as blind-box items, so you won’t know which one you’re getting until after you open it, unless you opt for the complete box set that guaranties you one of each version.

Individual Final Fantasy Series–Mini Melody TVs are priced at 1,980 yen (US$12.50) and the complete set at 11,880. They’re scheduled to officially go on sale on January 29.

title: American tourist in Japan arrested on charges of attempted murder and arson
description: Arrest follows Okinawan hotel fire that took place last month. Okinawa offers a wide range of activities for travelers to enjoy. It boasts Japan’s finest beaches, perfect for relaxing or marine sports such as snorkeling and scuba diving. The prefecture’s dense jungles offer ample hiking opportunities, and its unique Ryukyu cultural heritage can be experienced […]
content:
Arrest follows Okinawan hotel fire that took place last month.

Okinawa offers a wide range of activities for travelers to enjoy. It boasts Japan’s finest beaches, perfect for relaxing or marine sports such as snorkeling and scuba diving. The prefecture’s dense jungles offer ample hiking opportunities, and its unique Ryukyu cultural heritage can be experienced both at historical sites such as Shuri Castle and through the many restaurants serving traditional Okinawan cuisine.

Generally not recommended for visitors though? Arson and attempted murder, the activities for which one American tourist has been arrested on charges of.

In the pre-dawn hours of August 15, a fire broke out at Hamby Resort in the Chatan neighborhood of Okinawa City. The hotel, located a few blocks from both the shoreline and United States Marine Corps Camp Foster, had 19 guests staying in its trailer-style bungalows, close to full capacity during the busy Obon vacation period.

▼ Video of the fire

Thankfully, no lives were lost, although one guest, a 55-year-old man from Osaka, lost consciousness from smoke inhalation before being rescued by police and U.S. Marine Marshall Martinez, who saw the fire and volunteered to help. The man remains hospitalized in Okinawa.

Six days after the blaze, Posedion Roberson, a 32-year-old American tourist was arrested for trespassing into and sleeping inside a building complex in the town of Urasoe, roughly half an hour south of Chatan. Roberson, it turns out, had also booked a room at the hotel on the night of the fire, but disappeared after the incident, and investigators now believe he was the person responsible. On September 1, he was rearrested on charges of arson and attempted murder, and is currently in police custody.

▼ The hotel, prior to the fire

There’s been a noticeable uptick in high-profile crimes committed by foreign tourists in Japan over the past year or so, including vandalism, assault, and theft. Attempted mass murder, though, is on a whole other level, and if convicted, Roberson is unlikely to receive much in the way of clemency.

Source: Teleasa News, Okinawa Times, Stars and Stripes

title: Solo travel in Japan: $3 all-you-can-drink deal at this conveyor belt restaurant is a fun time for one
description: No need to feel self-conscious when you can use this automatic ordering and delivery system. Drinking in Tokyo on your own might sound like a daunting prospect for solo travellers in Japan, but if you know where to go it can be a fun time to remember, especially when it doesn’t break the bank. Our […]
content:
No need to feel self-conscious when you can use this automatic ordering and delivery system.

Drinking in Tokyo on your own might sound like a daunting prospect for solo travellers in Japan, but if you know where to go it can be a fun time to remember, especially when it doesn’t break the bank.

Our team of reporters are seasoned solo dining pros, always on the lookout for new places to eat and drink on their own, and their most recent find is one of the cheapest deals in town, letting you drink as much as you like for 90 minutes for the one-coin price of 500 yen (US$3.13).

The so-called “One-Coin All-You-Can-Drink” campaign comes from Yakiniku no Watami, a yakiniku chain that’s been taking over locations that formerly belonged to the now-phased-out Watami izakaya chain.

Our reporter Ahiruneko discovered the deal and immediately set out to try it, and when he arrived at his nearest branch shortly after midday, he was shown to a table seat as the solo seats at the counter were already full.

Settling into the booth, Ahiruneko was impressed by the setup – food is delivered via a “Special Express Lane” beside the table, and orders are made using a touchscreen panel.

▼ Like conveyor belt sushi, only with meat and alcohol.

Ahiruneko was here for the “One-Coin All-You-Can-Drink” deal, and sure enough it was being advertised with a laminated flyer at the table, which details of the 18 types of alcohol you can order over 90 minutes.

▼ Highballs, Sours, Gins and Mixers.

Bracing himself for the fine print, he looked closely at the details and was impressed again. Ahiruneko had assumed there would be restrictions like a table charge, an appetiser charge, or a requirement for at least two dishes per person, but the only real condition was ordering at least 500 yen worth of food, which was totally fine as he wouldn’t want to drink on an empty stomach anyway.

This is the full list of fine-print details:

・You need to order at least 500 yen worth of food (including tax)
・You can combine it with either an all-you-can-eat plan or individual dishes
・It can be ordered during either lunch or dinner hours
・You can also use the soft drink bar
・Last orders are 15 minutes before the 90-minute mark
・Draft beer is not included

You don’t often come across an all-you-can-drink deal with such easy requirements, so Ahiruneko wasted no time in ordering the “Watami Kalbi Lunch” for 1,089 yen, as the accompaniment for his day drinking.

When ordering his all-you-can-drink option, he found that he had to call a member of staff over first, as they needed to set up the touchscreen panel for the all-you-can-drink menu to appear.

▼ Highballs, lemon sours, tea-based drinks and Suntory Sui gin soda are some of the included options.

He made his selections and then, after waiting a little while…

▼ … his lunch and highball arrived on the lane.

The sight of his meal arriving, like a train pulling into a station, added a fantastic touch of excitement to his solo meal. Plucking his meal tray off the delivery tray, he saw that the Watami Kalbi was thicker than expected, making him one happy diner.

Giving it a light grill, Ahiruneko was very pleased with how his meal was turning out, and things got even better when he took a sip of his drink.

▼ Ahhhh, that hits the spot.

It didn’t take long for Ahiruneko to polish off his drink along with delicious bites of succulent meat, so he immediately ordered another beverage, and…

▼ … it arrived on the express lane.

This all-you-can-drink delivery system is one you don’t encounter very often, and it was Ahiruneko’s first time seeing it. Usually, even if you order by touchscreen, staff deliver drinks to your table, and as someone who feels slightly awkward with staff interactions, this system was ideal.

▼ In fact,  it was so ideal that he ended up downing seven drinks in 90 minutes.

Doing the math, that works out to about 71 yen ($0.46) per drink, which is pretty mind-blowing. Even when he factored in the meal cost, which brought the total to 1,589 yen, it was still a great deal that he would definitely go back for.

So in the end, Ahiruneko left the restaurant with a heavier belly, a lighter mood, and only a slightly lighter wallet. The one downside to the deal is it’s only available for a limited time until 17 September, and at limited locations, which we’ve listed for you below.

Participating Restaurants

Tokyo: Otorii Station Front, Kinshicho South Exit Station Front, Kokubunji South Exit, Chofu South Exit, Shimura-Sakaue, Ikebukuro East Exit, Kameari Station Front
Saitama: Kawagoe East Exit Crea Mall, Asakadai Station Front

title: Starbucks Japan adds new Sweet Potato Frappuccino and Latte to the menu, but do they deliver the taste of autumn?
description: New drinks coincide with the opening of the chain’s new “Customisation Bar”, giving us a hack for making them even better.   There’s now a distinct feeling of autumn in the air, and Starbucks is heralding its arrival in Japan with a very distinctive autumnal flavour: sweet potato. The ingredient is being showcased in two […]
content:
New drinks coincide with the opening of the chain’s new “Customisation Bar”, giving us a hack for making them even better.  

There’s now a distinct feeling of autumn in the air, and Starbucks is heralding its arrival in Japan with a very distinctive autumnal flavour: sweet potato. The ingredient is being showcased in two new drinks, the Torori Mitsuimo Beni Haruka Frappuccino and the Torori Mitsuimo Beni Haruka Mousse Tea Latte, which went on sale on 2 September.

With “torori” meaning “melty” or “gooey”, and “mitsuimo” (“honey potato”) referring to its thick sweetness, the Japanese names sound enticing to the ear, but would they be just as enticing to the palate? That was something our resident Starbucks expert, K. Masami, was keen to find out, so she lined up early when the drinks were released, and purchased them both for a tasting.

▼ She started the proceedings with the Tea Latte, which is sold in Small through to Venti sizes, from 640 yen (US$4.35).

The beauty of this drink lies in its many layers – take a preliminary sip and you’ll get a beautiful mouthful of honey-like sweetness from the chilled sweet potato paste in the base. Move the straw up slightly, and you’ll be able to enjoy a layer filled with milk tea, made with Darjeeling and Assam for a bold yet aromatic and refreshing astringency, before finishing with the fluffy mouthfeel of the sweet-potato-flavoured mousse topping.

As the drink contains a pre-blended tea mix, it can’t be customised with a different type of milk, so that’s something you might need to be aware of, but thankfully for Masami, that wasn’t a concern. After enjoying the layers separately she mixed them all together, and that’s when the beverage levelled up, taking on a richer, deeper flavour and consistency, and making every sip taste like Japanese autumn.

Masami loved the way Starbucks chose to use the Beni Haruka sweet potato variety, as it’s the one that’s most ubiquitous in Japan so it delivered all the familiar, nostalgic flavours from way back in her childhood. It worked a treat in the Frappuccino too, proudly showing off its sweet, rich flavour with the addition of crispy roasted sweet potato-flavoured pieces on top. These pieces are inspired by “imomitsu” (“potato honey”), which is the caramelised, honey-like juices that ooze out and harden on the surface of a sweet potato as it bakes, and they added an extra layer of authentic flavour to every mouthful.

▼ Frappuccino on the left

Another surprise awaiting customers from 2 September is the new “Customisation Bar”, which lets customers add various extras to their drinks, to personalise the flavours.

▼ The five optional add-ons are: Vanilla Sugar & Salt, Pepper Cardamom Maple Sauce, Ginger Sugar Chips, and Cinnamon Powder and Honey.

Masami had requested almond milk for her Frappuccino (the milk in the Frappuccino can be customised) so as she walked by the customisation bar, she couldn’t resist adding a sprinkling of cinnamon, which she thought might pair well with the slightly nutty flavour.

Taking a sip with the cinnamon made her fall even deeper in love with the Frappuccino, as it paired exceptionally well with the sweet potato. As a lover of spice, she would even go as far as to say that the drink felt complete after the cinnamon had been added, and she ended up wishing she’d tried it on the latte too.

There’s something about cinnamon that really helps to being things to life in a very autumnal way, so if you do get to order one of these drinks, she highly recommends adding it if you can. It’ll really get you in the mood for all things autumn, and with a very distinctive seasonal ingredient as the main star, the flavour of Japanese autumn will stay with you as a fond memory after the very last sip.
